chapter_en: Holy and Mundane in Settling the Land

sections.title_en: The Inheritance of Reuven and Gad, and the Flaw in Their Intention
sections.body_en:
Originally Moshe our teacher did not intend to conquer the eastern bank of the Jordan; although it is part of the Land of Israel, the intention was to settle first in the land of Kena'an, which is on the western side of the Jordan and is more sanctified, and from there to grow strong and spread out to all the borders of the Land. But Siḥon and Og went out to war against Israel, and Israel defeated them and conquered their land (see Bamidbar 21:21-35, and Ramban there 21, and see below 3:18).

And when the children of Reuven and the children of Gad, who had very great and numerous livestock, saw that the territories of the eastern bank of the Jordan were good for livestock, they came before Moshe with a request that he not bring them across the Jordan, but give them their inheritance on the eastern bank of the Jordan.

The answer of Moshe our teacher was surprising in its severity. First he flung at them: "Shall your brothers go to war, and shall you sit here?!" (Bamidbar 32:6). He further went on to accuse them of repeating the sin of the spies, who despised the Land of Israel and discouraged the heart of the people from going into the Land, and aroused great wrath against Israel, until on their account it was decreed that all the members of that generation would die in the wilderness. And here they now arise to cause Israel to sin again and to weaken them so that they will not enter the Land, and perhaps they too, like the spies, will cause a terrible disaster. And he expanded in words of rebuke, without asking them whether their intention was indeed not to take part with Israel in the conquest of the Land (Bamidbar 32:7-15).

After Moshe finished his words of rebuke, the children of Reuven and Gad answered and said that they had no intention of evading the war; rather, they would build sheepfolds for their livestock and cities for their little ones, and would go out as a vanguard before Israel to conquer the whole Land. And only after all the tribes had finished inheriting their inheritance would they return to their land on the eastern bank of the Jordan. Seemingly, after these words Moshe our teacher should have made peace with them, and perhaps even apologised to them for having suspected them. But although Moshe agreed that if they indeed crossed over as a vanguard before Israel they would be clear before God and before Israel, it appeared from his words that he feared they would not keep their word, and therefore he again demanded that they commit themselves once more, in detail and with a double condition, to their undertaking to take part in the conquest of the Land.

Seemingly one should ask about Moshe our teacher: why did he not listen to the children of Reuven and Gad until the end of their words? Why did he begin to rebuke them with harsh words and grave accusations, without first clarifying whether they were willing to take part in the conquest of the Land? And why, after they told him that they were willing to take part in the conquest of the Land, did he continue to treat them with suspicion?

The answer is that there was a basic flaw in their desire to inherit the eastern bank of the Jordan. Their order of values was distorted. For it was not because they felt an inner affinity to the eastern bank of the Jordan, in which they would be able to realise the vision particular to them for revealing God's name in the world, that they wanted to inherit the eastern bank of the Jordan; it was only because they were concerned for their wealth that they wanted to inherit it. And Moshe our teacher knew that when the first motive for settling the Land does not stem from the supreme value of realising the covenant with the Holy One, blessed be He, and revealing the Shekhina in the Land, their hold on the Land will be loose, and heaven forbid the Land may not endure in their hands.1

Therefore, even after they undertook to go out as a vanguard before Israel, Moshe still treated them with suspicion. For indeed, after they undertook to take part in the conquest of the Land, they had permission to inherit the eastern bank of the Jordan, which is also the Land of Israel. But if they did not elevate their aim, and intend to inherit the Land together with all Israel for the sake of revealing the word of God in the world, they would not be able to endure.

And as our Sages said (Bamidbar Rabba 22:7), there are rich people who do not understand that wealth is a gift of Heaven, and are drawn after their money, and in the end they are lost from the world together with their money. "And so you find with the children of Gad and the children of Reuven, who were rich and had great livestock, and they loved their money and settled outside the Land of Israel; therefore they were exiled first of all the tribes, as it is said (I Divrei Ha-yamim 5:26): And he carried them away, the Reuvenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Menashe. And who caused it for them? Because they separated themselves from their brothers for the sake of their possessions." (The intention of our Sages in "outside the Land of Israel" is outside the principal holiness of the Land, as explained below 3:2; 3:13.)2

notes_en.en: This came to expression also in their putting their wealth before their families, for thus they asked of Moshe: "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones" (Bamidbar 32:16). And the Sages said (Rashi, based on Tanḥuma 7): "They cared more for their money than for their sons and daughters, for they mentioned their livestock before their little ones." Therefore Moshe corrected them and said: "Build cities for your little ones" and afterwards "and folds for your sheep" (ibid. 24).

They still had an opportunity to repent: after the conquest of the Land was completed, when they returned to the other side of the Jordan, they felt that their land was less sanctified, and they set up an altar for themselves on the eastern bank of the Jordan. And Yehoshua bin Nun warned them not to set up an altar there (and this is the main difference between the two banks of the Jordan, as our Sages said in Bamidbar Rabba 7:8: "The land of Kena'an is fit for the house of the Shekhina, and the other side of the Jordan is not fit for the house of the Shekhina"). And about this Yehoshua said to them (Yehoshua 22:19): "But if the land of your possession is unclean, then pass over to the land of the possession of the Lord, where the Tabernacle of the Lord dwells, and take possession among us; but do not rebel against the Lord, nor rebel against us, by building yourselves an altar besides the altar of the Lord our God." But even then they did not repent, and in the end they were exiled first, and about this Shlomo proclaimed (Mishlei 20:21): "An inheritance hastily gotten at the beginning, its end shall not be blessed" (see Bamidbar Rabba 22:9).

sections.body_en:
The first city that Israel conquered in the land of Kena'an was Yeriḥo. Yeriḥo expresses to a great extent the essence of Canaanite culture, and all the honey of the Land of Israel came to expression in Yeriḥo. Therefore Yehoshua sent spies to see "the land and Yeriḥo" (Yehoshua 2:1); thus Yeriḥo was equal to the whole Land of Israel, as our Sages said: "for it was as hard as all of them" (Sifrei Devarim 52), and "it was equal to all of them" (Yalkut Shimoni, Yehoshua 8).

Originally the whole valley around the Dead Sea was like the garden of the Lord, and therefore Lot chose to live there. But in the wake of the sins of Sedom and Amora, who loved their wealth and trusted in it until they became utterly wicked, Sedom and Amora were overturned, and the good soil turned into a desolate wilderness, and the sweet waters turned salty, in which no fish can live. And of all those good places only Yeriḥo remained, flourishing and thriving, an oasis unique of its kind, whose delicious fruits all the kings of the world desired to enjoy.

But the enormous physical abundance that was in Yeriḥo and in all the land of Kena'an, without a spiritual counterweight, may sweep a person away to material desires and idolatry. The source of this enormous abundance is in the holiness of the Land; but when one does not grasp the spiritual root of the abundance, the physical desires prevail, and then a much greater corruption is created. For this is not ordinary materialism, but materialism that grows stronger and intensifies through the spirituality that becomes an instrument in its service. Therefore the Canaanites were more abominable in their deeds than all the nations (Sifra Aḥarei 9; Maharal, Gevurot Hashem chapter 4). And this is what happened to the people of Sedom and Amora.

The aim of the Land of Israel is to reveal the word of God in spirituality and in physicality; therefore the abundance of the Land of Israel is expressed in the ability to receive prophecy in it, and in the Land's flowing with milk and honey. But great care is needed not to be swept after physicality and be separated from the spiritual root, to the point of destruction.

The essence of the Canaanite tendency to be swept after physicality was in Yeriḥo. Therefore the war against it was hard and spiritual: forces of holiness against the seven impure kelipot (husks) that were in Kena'an. And therefore they went around the city seven times, seven circuits of faith, with the ark of the covenant of the Lord at the head of the camp; and by the power of the blowing of the shofarot and the shout of all Israel before God, the walls of Yeriḥo fell and the children of Israel captured the city. And from here the way was opened to conquer the whole Land.3

notes_en.en: Even before the conquest of Yeriḥo, the spies succeeded in bringing about the repentance of Raḥav the harlot and her conversion, and so the holy spark within the kelipa of Kena'an returned to Judaism. As long as Raḥav did not know Israel, the holy spark within her aroused her to mighty searching. And since she knew only this world, she searched within it, and according to the greatness of her strength was the greatness of her sins. But as soon as she saw the spies, she recognised the way of truth and said that the Lord is God in the heavens above and on the earth below (Yehoshua 2:11). And she rose so high that Yehoshua bin Nun married her, and eight prophets came forth from her (Megilla 14b).

sections.body_en:
Now it is understood why Yehoshua decreed that all the spoil of Yeriḥo would be ḥerem, holy to the Lord (Yehoshua 6:17-19): so that the first step of Israel in the Land would be clean of every physical inclination, and thereby to establish in the hearts that the conquest of the Land is not for material aims alone, but first and foremost for the sake of building the Temple. Therefore he also decreed that they not build Yeriḥo as a permanent building. "And Yehoshua adjured them at that time, saying: Cursed be the man before the Lord who rises up and builds this city, Yeriḥo; with his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and with his youngest son shall he set up its gates" (ibid. 26). All this so that rich and fertile Yeriḥo would not become a city competing with Shilo and Jerusalem. And so Israel conducted themselves for generations: some of the pilgrims would come to Yeriḥo, and from there they would supply good food to those going up to Jerusalem, and so the honey of Yeriḥo assisted the service of God in the Temple.4

Therefore the sin of Akhan, who coveted a mantle of Shin'ar and silver and gold, was so grave, for he damaged the holy aim of the conquest of the Land. And our Sages hinted that by his deed he caused the first crack that afterwards led to the destruction of the Land. For that mantle of Shin'ar belonged to the king of Bavel (Bereshit Rabba 85:14). And so, after many years, when the sins grew, one of his descendants, Nevukhadnetzar king of Bavel, was able to destroy the Temple and exile Israel. For he could argue that from the outset Israel had not entered the Land for the sake of Heaven, but Israel is like all the nations, and just as all the nations are built and destroyed, so too Israel.

In one of the evil periods, in which Israel inclined after desires and worshipped idols, they transgressed the oath of Yehoshua and built the city of Yeriḥo, and this was an expression of their inclining after physicality and turning their backs on the holiness in Jerusalem. "And Aḥav did yet more to provoke the Lord, God of Israel, than all the kings of Israel who were before him. In his days Ḥiel of Beit-El (who was his treasurer) built Yeriḥo; with Aviram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and with Seguv his youngest son he set up its gates, according to the word of the Lord which He spoke by the hand of Yehoshua bin Nun" (I Melakhim 16:33-34).

One may say that the reality of the destruction of Sedom and Amora expresses the fact that we are not yet able to sanctify materiality completely; therefore, had Israel entered the Land when the whole plain of the Jordan was fertile like the garden of Eden, there would have been a great concern that they would be drawn after the abundance of physicality and forget to go up to Jerusalem and build the Temple in it.

And in the future to come, when the world is repaired, a river will go forth from the Temple, and its waters will increase and rise until they reach the eastern sea, which is the Dead Sea, and they will heal its waters, and fish will multiply in it greatly, and the wilderness will again become like the garden of Eden. "And by the river upon its bank, on this side and on that side, shall grow every tree for food, whose leaf shall not wither, nor shall its fruit fail; it shall bring forth new fruit every month, because its waters issue from the Sanctuary; and its fruit shall be for food, and its leaf for healing" (Yeḥezkel 47:12). And this will be an expression of the complete revelation of the word of God, in heaven and on earth, in unity, as it is said (Zekharya 14:9): "And the Lord shall be King over all the earth; on that day the Lord shall be one and His name one."

notes_en.en: One can further perceive the special connection between Jerusalem and Yeriḥo from what our Sages said (Yoma 39b): that the sound of the opening of the doors of the Sanctuary in Jerusalem was heard in Yeriḥo, and the goats in Yeriḥo would sneeze from the scent of the incense in Jerusalem. And even the women in Yeriḥo did not need to perfume themselves, because of the scent of the incense. And the Ra'avad explained on Mishna Tamid chapter 3 that this was something special in Yeriḥo, which had a special miraculous connection with Jerusalem, but other places that were nearer did not hear the sound of the doors and did not smell the incense.

sections.title_en: The Response of Shmuel the Prophet to the Request for a King
sections.body_en:
Shmuel the prophet is considered the greatest of the prophets of Israel after Moshe our teacher. The Sages said (Ta'anit 5b) that in a certain respect Shmuel was equal to Moshe and Aharon, as it is said (Tehillim 99:6): "Moshe and Aharon among His kohanim, and Shmuel among those who call upon His name." For through Moshe and Aharon God's guidance was revealed in the spiritual life that Israel had in the wilderness, whereas Shmuel continued to reveal the word of God in the life of the Land of Israel. By the power of the mighty activity of Shmuel, who went around the cities of Israel and taught Torah with unparalleled self-sacrifice, the people was aroused to repent, great blessing spread, and after long years in which the Philistines had subjugated Israel, by the power of Shmuel's leadership Israel prevailed over the Philistines and subdued them and restored the cities they had taken from Israel, and the Philistines came no more into the border of Israel all the days of Shmuel (I Shmuel chapter 7).

And it came to pass when Shmuel was old, and his sons did not walk in his ways, that all the elders of Israel gathered together and said to Shmuel: "Behold, you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways; now make us a king to judge us like all the nations." Shmuel's reaction was harsh: "But the thing displeased Shmuel when they said: Give us a king to judge us. And Shmuel prayed to the Lord. And the Lord said to Shmuel: Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me from reigning over them. According to all the deeds which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt to this day, in that they forsook Me and served other gods, so they do also to you. Now therefore listen to their voice; however, you shall solemnly warn them, and shall tell them the manner of the king who shall reign over them" (I Shmuel 8:4-9).

And indeed Shmuel warns them of the great power placed in the king's hand, which may lead the kingdom to tyranny and corruption, until the people cry out to God to save them from the king's hand. "But the people refused to listen to the voice of Shmuel, and they said: No, but there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles" (ibid. 8:19-20). Shmuel still hoped that God would prevent the people from choosing a king, but God said to him: listen to their voice. And Shmuel began the process of choosing the king, at the end of which Saul was chosen, who hid himself among the baggage out of humility. "And they ran and fetched him from there, and when he stood among the people he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders and upward. And Shmuel said to all the people: Do you see him whom the Lord has chosen, that there is none like him among all the people? And all the people shouted and said: Long live the king" (ibid. 10:23-24). But there were worthless men who despised him and brought him no gift, because he was too modest for their taste.

In time Naḥash the Ammonite came to subjugate the inhabitants of Yavesh Gil'ad, and Saul summoned the people and waged a successful war against him, and the people was filled with admiration for Saul its king. "Then Shmuel said to the people: Come and let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom there. And all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the Lord in Gilgal, and there they sacrificed peace offerings before the Lord, and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly."

And suddenly, in the midst of the great rejoicing, Shmuel the prophet burst out with harsh and terrible words. First he turned to the people and said: you asked for a king, and behold I have listened to your voice and will make a king for you. And I have walked before you from my youth to this day; tell me before God and before your king: during all these days did I ever receive from any of you a benefit for my devoted service to you? Did I take a bribe from any of you? Did I defraud any of you? And they all answered: Heaven forbid! You have not defrauded us, nor taken anything from any man's hand. Then Shmuel began to say to them harsh words of rebuke: how God always did kindness with them, and they time after time went astray after other gods. And when calamity came upon them in the wake of their sins, they would return and cry out to God, and God would save them. And suddenly now they rejoice in the king they have chosen, as though by his merit they had been saved from their enemies. And he went on to warn them that if they truly fear God and serve Him, they and their king will endure, but if they do not listen to the voice of God, the hand of God will be against them and against their king. And his mind was not at rest until he said: is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call to God that He send thunder and rain, so that you will see how great your wickedness is in asking for a king.

"So Shmuel called to the Lord, and the Lord sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared the Lord and Shmuel. And all the people said to Shmuel: Pray for your servants to the Lord your God, that we die not, for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king. And Shmuel said to the people: Fear not; you have done all this evil, yet do not turn aside from following the Lord, but serve the Lord with all your heart. And do not turn aside, for then you would go after vain things which cannot profit nor save, for they are vain. For the Lord will not forsake His people for His great name's sake, because it has pleased the Lord to make you a people for Himself. Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you; but I will teach you the good and the right way. Only fear the Lord and serve Him in truth with all your heart, for consider what great things He has done for you. But if you still do evil, you shall be swept away, both you and your king" (ibid. 12:18-25).

Seemingly one should ask: why did Shmuel suddenly become indignant against them, since he had already agreed to appoint a king for them; why did he again rebuke them with harsh words? But he knew that, since their aim in asking for a king was not for the sake of Heaven, the end of the kingdom would be that it would be destroyed and Israel would be exiled from their land. For such is the nature of every physical thing, that in the end it wastes away, and only Israel live and endure, because their root is spiritual. And since their request for the king stemmed from physical motives alone, in the end everything would be destroyed. Over this Shmuel grieved so greatly. And in order to prevent the disaster that might come, Shmuel directed his rebuke.

Indeed the kingdom of Saul fell. But Shmuel, on the mission of God, appointed as king his fellow who was better than he, David, and commanded him to prepare the building of the Temple, in order to establish in Israel the status of holiness, which is above everything. And David tried to repair the flaw, and therefore he did not feel at ease when he lived in a house of cedar while the ark of God remained within a tabernacle of curtains. But the prophet said to him in the name of God that although Israel had not acted properly in delaying the building of the Temple, on the other hand one should not build the Temple in haste; therefore his son, who would continue his kingdom, would build the Temple (II Shmuel chapter 7).

King Shlomo fulfilled his father's instruction and built the Temple. And he even hastened and made haste to complete the house of God in seven years, whereas his palace he finished in thirteen years. And this had great significance, because the king's palace included within it all the components of government, like in our day the government ministries and the Knesset together. And Shlomo first finished building the Temple, to teach the whole people that the Temple comes before the kingdom.

And nevertheless, the original flaw was not completely repaired: Shmuel's fear was realised, the first aim of the request for a king like all the nations prevailed, the service of God did not occupy the central place in the life of the people and the kingdom, sins increased and the kingdom became corrupt, until the Temple was destroyed and the Land was destroyed and Israel were exiled from their land. And only the spiritual heritage of the prophets and the righteous kings remained in the hearts.

sections.title_en: The Reward of Those Who Settle the Land: Omri and Aḥav
sections.body_en:
Come and see how great is the virtue of the mitzva of settling the Land, that even the wicked who engage in building it merit reward. As Tanna De-vei Eliyahu said (Eliyahu Rabba chapter 9): "Once I was sitting in the great study hall in Jerusalem before the Sages, and I asked them: Why was King Omri different, that all the kings before him did not merit to seat their sons after them on the throne of their kingdom, whereas Omri merited to seat three kings of his seed on his throne? They said to me: We have not heard. I said to them: My masters, Omri merited to seat three kings on his throne because he built a great city in the Land of Israel."

That is to say, although King Omri did evil in the eyes of the Lord more than all who were before him (I Melakhim 16:25), the merit of the mitzva of settling the Land stood for him and for his seed, and by its merit he established three kings of his seed on the throne of his kingdom, which the other kings of Israel did not merit. And all this although he did not build the city out of pure intentions of settling the Land, but had personal motives to fortify the standing of his kingdom. For thus Omri said: just as Jerusalem is for the kings of Yehuda, so shall Shomron be for the kings of Israel. From here we learn how great is the virtue of the mitzva of settling the Land, that although there was a significant flaw in Omri's motive in building the city of Shomron, since in practice he settled the Land, he merited to establish three kings of his seed on his throne (Aḥav his son, Aḥazyahu son of Aḥav, Yoram son of Aḥav).

The mitzva of settling the Land is bound up with the unity of the people, and in the days of Aḥav peace was made between the kingdom of Yehuda and the kingdom of Israel; Yehoram son of Yehoshafat king of Yehuda married the daughter of Aḥav, and the king of Yehuda and the king of Israel would go out together to war against their enemies (I Melakhim 22). And so our Sages said that the generation of Aḥav were idol worshippers, and nevertheless they would go out to war and win, because they did not speak lashon ha-ra. Whereas the generation of Shaul were people of Torah, and nevertheless they would go out to war and fall, because there were speakers of lashon ha-ra among them (Devarim Rabba 5:10; Yerushalmi Pe'ah 1:1). And so it is brought in the Sifrei (Bamidbar piska 42): "Great is peace, for even if Israel worship idols and there is peace among them, so to speak the Omnipresent says: the Satan does not touch them, as it is said (Hoshe'a 4:17): Efrayim is joined to idols, let him alone. But once they are divided, what is said of them (ibid. 10:2)? Their heart is divided; now they shall bear their guilt."

And so we find that Aḥav honoured the Torah. That is, although he was a sinner and transgressed all the transgressions in the Torah,5 out of national feeling he honoured the Torah. And so it is told that when Ben-Hadad king of Aram prevailed over him and besieged Shomron, he demanded that he give him his silver and his gold and his wives and his children. And Aḥav, who thought his chances of winning the battle were lost, surrendered and agreed to give everything that belonged to him personally to the king of Aram. But when Ben-Hadad went on to demand the delight of his eyes, which the Sages explained (Sanhedrin 102b) meant the Torah scroll, he did not agree. The national honour, expressed in the honour of the Torah scroll, which is a sanctified national possession, was so precious to him that he preferred to go out to a lost battle rather than humiliate the honour of Israel by handing the Torah scroll into the enemy's hands. And since this was a fateful decision, on account of which many might die, he did not want to decide it alone and consulted the elders, and they too strengthened him in his decision not to surrender and humiliate the honour of Israel. And a prophet came in the name of God to advise Aḥav how to win. And the children of Israel went out and struck Aram a great blow. And the prophet came in the name of God to warn him that the next year Ben-Hadad would again come against him to war. And Aḥav prepared his army properly for war, and Israel again defeated Aram (I Melakhim 20:1-30).

notes_en.en: See also Sanhedrin 113a: after Ḥiel, Aḥav's friend, built a city and called it Yeriḥo and buried his sons, Aḥav complained about Ḥiel's punishment, and said insolently that he himself worshipped idols in every place and nevertheless rain falls. Then Eliyahu swore that neither dew nor rain would fall.

sections.title_en: Without Faith, Love of the Land and the People Also Fades
sections.body_en:
But one must know that the merit of the mitzva of settling the Land, and the unity that stems from national feeling, cannot stand forever. And since Omri sinned in idolatry, and his son Aḥav sinned yet more than all the kings of Israel who were before him (I Melakhim 16:30-33; 21:25), and so did his two sons, their attitude to the people and the Land also grew weaker and weaker, until in the end calamity came upon them.

Thus it happened to Aḥav: as a result of his distance from God and from the Torah, he weakened also in his national stance. After he succeeded, by the kindness of God, in defeating Aram, instead of killing Ben-Hadad as he had schemed to do to Israel, he had pity on him, raised him into his chariot, made a covenant with him and sent him away free. And the prophet came, "and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Because you have let go out of your hand the man whom I had devoted to destruction, therefore your life shall go for his life, and your people for his people" (ibid. 20:42). And so it was: a few years later Aḥav was killed in the war against Aram (ibid. 22:34-38).

Forsaking God also brought about moral decline, which came to sharp expression in Aḥav's treatment of Navot the Yizre'elite. Aḥav coveted his vineyard, and when Navot would not agree to sell it to him, on the advice of his wicked wife Izevel false witnesses were brought who testified against Navot that he had rebelled against the king. In the wake of their testimony Navot was executed and Aḥav inherited his vineyard. And God commanded Eliyahu the prophet: "Arise, go down to meet Aḥav king of Israel, who is in Shomron; behold, he is in the vineyard of Navot, where he has gone down to take possession of it. And you shall speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord: Have you murdered and also taken possession?! And you shall speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord: In the place where the dogs licked the blood of Navot shall the dogs lick your blood, even yours" (I Melakhim 21:17-19).

The root of the calamity of the house of Omri began in their inclining after idolatry. And Aḥav sinned yet more than all the kings before him: he forsook the Torah and the mitzvot, inclined after idolatry, took as wife Izevel daughter of Etba'al king of the Tzidonim, set up a temple and an altar for the Ba'al in Shomron, and destroyed the altars of God (ibid. 16). When the prophets of God stood up to rebuke him, he murdered them, until only Eliyahu the prophet remained alone of all the prophets of God (ibid. 19:10). Then a harsh and terrible decree was decreed upon the house of Aḥav, as God said to Eliyahu the prophet: "Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus, and when you come, anoint Ḥazael to be king over Aram. And Yehu son of Nimshi you shall anoint to be king over Israel, and Elisha son of Shafat of Avel Meḥola you shall anoint to be prophet in your place. And it shall be that whoever escapes the sword of Ḥazael, Yehu shall slay; and whoever escapes the sword of Yehu, Elisha shall slay" (ibid. 19:15-17). But as long as the merit of settling the Land and national responsibility still stood for them, they won in their wars, and they could still repent and annul the decree that hovered over them. But they did not repent, and over time their attitude to the people and the Land also grew weaker and weaker, and the terrible calamity that had been decreed upon them was fulfilled.

First Ḥazael king of Aram began to strike Yehoram son of Aḥav (II Melakhim 8:28). After that Elisha the prophet sent one of the sons of the prophets to anoint Yehu as king, and commanded him in the name of God to rebel against Yehoram son of Aḥav, and to strike and destroy the whole house of Aḥav (ibid. 9:6-10). And Yehu rebelled against Yehoram son of Aḥav, "and he struck all that remained to Aḥav in Shomron, until he had destroyed him, according to the word of the Lord which He spoke to Eliyahu" (ibid. 10:17).

Throughout all the years of exile, Israel continued to yearn for their Land. The outstanding among the great ones of the generations, such as R. Yehuda Ha-levi, the Rambam and the Ramban, even fulfilled the mitzva themselves and went up to the Land. But the hour had not yet come for God to remember His people, and Israel too did not repent and did not make proper effort to go up to the Land, and consequently the Jewish settlement in the Land did not succeed in strengthening and establishing itself.

More than two hundred years ago, a renewed awakening to go up to the Land began. An early glimmer occurred in the aliya of Rabbi Ḥayim ben Attar, the greatest of the rabbis in Morocco, author of the commentary Or Ha-ḥayim on the Torah, who mentioned explicitly that this aliya involves inheriting the Land and bringing the redemption near (and see also his commentary on Vayikra 25:25). After that, in the year 5537 (1777), the greatest of the disciples of the Maggid of Mezeritch, the Admor Rabbi Menaḥem Mendel of Vitebsk, went up to the Land, and with him three hundred olim. Then the foundation was laid for the Ḥasidic communities in the Land.

But the one who spoke most explicitly about going up to the Land and building it was the Gaon Rabbi Eliyahu of Vilna. His disciples related that many times he would speak with them in a storm of soul, that only through the ingathering of the exiles and the building of the Land will the redemption be hastened, and only through the building of the Land will we be saved from the terrible sufferings of the birth pangs of the Messiah. Apparently the Gra foresaw in his mind's eye what was liable to come upon European Jewry. He himself also set out on his way to the Land, and even took leave of his household in a letter of testament, but from Heaven he was instructed to return, and he returned. But he continued to encourage his disciples to go up to the Land and build it.

In the year 5569 (1809), about ten years after the passing of the Gra, the first group of his disciples went up to Tzfat, headed by Rabbi Menaḥem Mendel of Shklov. About two years after him Rabbi Yisrael of Shklov, author of the book Pe'at Ha-shulḥan, went up. With them was Rabbi Hillel of Shklov, and other great ones in Torah and deed. Over time many of them moved to live in Jerusalem. Terrible troubles befell them, but they strengthened themselves in the words of their great teacher about the importance of the mitzva of settling the Land. And so from generation to generation they increased and multiplied and became established in the Land, and from them was founded the principal Ashkenazi 'Old Yishuv' in the Land, and by their strength the first neighbourhoods of Jerusalem outside the wall were built, and from them came forth the founders of the 'New Yishuv', such as Petaḥ Tikva. From a few hundred righteous Jews who went up to the Land with self-sacrifice beyond compare, within less than a hundred years they multiplied to tens of thousands. But we did not merit that the masses of the house of Israel would follow in their footsteps, and the troubles of exile grew and grew.

About fifty years after the awakening of the Gra's disciples, Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Kalischer and Rabbi Eliyahu Guttmacher arose, two of the great ones of the generation, disciples of Rabbi Akiva Eiger, and began to encourage mass aliya for the sake of building the Jewish kingdom in the Land of Israel. In the wake of their words the olim to the Land increased. But we were still far from attaining the general goal, and the troubles of exile grew and grew, antisemitism intensified, the process of abandoning religion also accelerated, and many Jews began to assimilate in the Diaspora.

Several decades later some of the great ones of Israel from Eastern Europe arose, among them Rabbi Shmuel Mohilever, Rabbi Mordekhai Eliasberg and the head of the Volozhin yeshiva, Rabbi Naftali Tzvi Yehuda Berlin (the Netziv), to encourage aliya to the Land within the framework of the Ḥibbat Tziyon movement. In that period the Jews who had left the way of Torah and mitzvot had already multiplied. And those great ones agreed to join with public leaders who were not careful in observing mitzvot for the sake of the goal of settling the Land. In the wake of their activity the aliya called 'the First' arose (from the year 5642 onward, 1882). Most of the olim then were observant, but they were far from the level of the Gra's disciples, who were geniuses and righteous men. Indeed among the olim then too there were important Torah scholars, such as Rabbi Mordekhai Gimpel Jaffe (the great-uncle of Rav Kook), who joined the moshava of Yehud and became its rabbi. And although by the merit of this aliya the Yishuv grew and grew, the masses of the house of Israel still did not respond to the call to return to Tziyon.

Antisemitism in Europe grew and grew, and the number of Jews who stopped keeping Torah and mitzvot also continued to grow. Many of those who left hoped that with their leaving religion and assimilating among the nations their troubles would end. But antisemitism grew stronger. Among some of the Jews who tried to integrate among the nations the recognition became clear that the Jewish character is unique and it is impossible to escape it, and only by establishing an independent Jewish state in the Land of Israel would it be possible to save the Jews from the antisemitism that was growing ever stronger. Thus the Zionist movement arose, headed by Binyamin Ze'ev Herzl. There were among the great ones of Israel who supported it; in time they organised within the framework of the Mizraḥi movement. There were among the great ones who opposed the Zionist movement, chiefly because they feared that the masses of the people would be drawn after the ways of life of its secular leaders.

The Zionist idea, combined with growing antisemitism, roused larger groups of Jews to support aliya and the expansion of settlement and to demand the establishment of a Jewish state. But the truth must be told: most of the Jewish people, religious and secular alike, did not take part in the Zionist movement.

Only after the Holocaust was it already clear to many of the Jewish people that an independent Jewish state must be established in the Land of Israel. Masses of refugees from Europe and from the Arab lands went up to the Land, and thus the State of Israel arose and became established.

sections.title_en: The Necessity of Returning to Holiness
sections.body_en:
Many knocks did the Holy One, blessed be He, knock on the door of Knesset Yisrael, to rouse her to return to her Land. Had we merited to respond to the call of the Gra and his disciples, one cannot describe from how many pogroms and calamities we would have been saved. The Jewish people too would have remained more connected to Torah and mitzvot, for the masses of the house of Israel would have seen with their own eyes how by the merit of the Torah's guidance life is built properly. The abandonment of the Torah stemmed from a feeling that whoever is bound to it remains behind. The whole world was engaged in establishing new states and regimes, whereas Judaism was engaged in survival, under conditions that grew harder from year to year. Had we been engaged in building the people and the Land, the great vision of the ingathering of exiles and the building of the Land, as the words of the prophets in the light of the Torah, would have filled the hearts. All the talented Jews who assimilated and gave their strength to strangers, in science, in culture, in statecraft and in economics, would have invested their energy in the Land, for the sake of their people and their homeland. The Jewish state would have arisen earlier, not from the pressure of troubles but out of the mitzva of the Torah and the vision of the prophets. Even the problems with the Arab population would have been negligible, for only because we did not come here in masses was room created for many Arabs to migrate to the Land in recent generations.

Even after the aliya of the Gra's disciples, we still had many opportunities to awaken. Some went up, but the overwhelming majority remained in exile. Only after the Holocaust did a large Jewish public awaken to aliya and the settling of the Land. And the Land responded to all who went up to it, and gave its fruits in abundance to the children returning from afar.

Historical reality has proven that those who acted in recent generations for the sake of building the Land of Israel and saving the people of Israel, religious and secular alike, merited blessing. From Heaven we were given a hint that the hour had come to return to the Land. What was built in the Land in recent generations endured and flourished; what was built outside the Land collapsed and crumbled. The words of the prophet were fulfilled, which the Gra and his disciples often mentioned: "For in Mount Tziyon and in Jerusalem there shall be a remnant that escapes" (Yo'el 3:5). Many of those who led the building of the Land merited greatness, even though they did not always do so for the sake of Heaven, and at times even set pioneering against the observance of Torah and mitzvot.

But the merit of this precious mitzva does not stand forever. Without faith in God and cleaving to the Torah and the mitzvot, we will not be able to continue settling the Land with the proper devotion, and calamity may come. As our teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-kohen Kook zt"l used to tell about his father, our master Rav Kook zt"l, that several times he heard him say with actual weeping: "I am afraid of what our Sages said about the three generations before the coming of the redeemer, about whom it is said: You grew fat, you grew thick, you became gross." And the intention is that out of the lack of connection to holiness, they become more and more defiled, and by force of this come terrible calamities of the birth pangs of the Messiah, which are meant to return us to the path of repentance and redemption.6

We pray that we merit to connect to the sanctified root of settling the Land according to the aim of the Gra's disciples and their successors, Rav Kalischer and his colleagues, and out of this build our state in the light of the Torah's guidance, and merit complete redemption speedily in our days, amen.

notes_en.en:
Devarim 32:15: "But Yeshurun grew fat and kicked; you grew fat, you grew thick, you became gross; then he forsook God who made him, and scorned the Rock of his salvation." The Sages said (Sifrei Devarim piska 318): "You grew fat, you grew thick, you became gross: these are the three generations before the days of the Messiah, as it is said (Yeshayahu 2:7-8): And his land is full of horses, and there is no end to his chariots; and his land is full of silver and gold, and there is no end to his treasures; and his land is full of idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to that which their own fingers have made." To understand the matter I will bring the whole passage there, Yeshayahu 2:5-11: "O house of Ya'akov, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord… And his land is full of silver and gold, and there is no end to his treasures; and his land is full of horses, and there is no end to his chariots. And his land is full of idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to that which their own fingers have made. And man is bowed down, and man is brought low; therefore do not forgive them. Enter into the rock, and hide in the dust, from before the terror of the Lord and from the glory of His majesty. The lofty looks of man shall be brought low, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day."
In letter 144, from the year 5668, our master the Rav called on the loyal and faithful of Israel to build the Land in spirit and in body, combining Torah with derekh eretz, for the whole future of building the Land and the sprouting of the horn of salvation depends on building the Land out of true fear of Heaven. For if not, those with "the high hand armed with licentiousness and the ways of the nations will take control, with no remembrance of the true holiness of Israel, which covers its potsherds with the dross of a counterfeit nationalism, with grains of history and of love of the language, which clothes life in an Israelite form on the outside where the inside is wholly not Jewish, which is destined to be turned into a destroyer and a monster, and in the end also into hatred of Israel and of the Land of Israel, as we have already seen from experience. (If) this impure hand prevails, then there is not enough to explain the greatness of the disaster. But in God I have trusted, that He will not let our foot slip, and everyone who trembles at the word of God, and everyone who desires the salvation of His people and His holy Land, will stand by our banner, and we will begin to lay in Tziyon a precious cornerstone, and to revive the New Yishuv on the basis of the purity of faith, joined with the joy of life and the pursuit of its just aspirations, and God will be with us, to raise up the ruins of our people for all generations."
